title: Testing Claude with a structured macro context layer after today’s PCE release
author: cocopierlab
selftext:
I’ve been building **FX Context**, an MCP service for trading agents.

After today’s US PCE release, I asked Claude:

>Use FX Context to get the latest US PCE.

The screenshot shows the actual response.

The service returned the latest PCE release, including headline/core MoM and YoY values, plus derived values from the underlying index levels.

One useful thing this test exposed: this release didn’t yet have a consensus block in my service, so no surprise could be calculated.

The workflow I’m aiming for is:

`actual → consensus → surprise → market reaction → agent reasoning`

I’d rather keep those calculations deterministic and let the model focus on interpretation.

One thing I’m still testing: if I simply ask Claude “What’s the latest US PCE?”, it doesn’t always choose the MCP automatically. If I explicitly say “Use FX Context”, it does.

For people building AI trading systems: do you prefer giving the model raw macro data, or a normalized context layer like this?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: I’d prefer the normalized layer, but it should preserve enough provenance for Claude to distinguish “not available” from “not found.” In this August 2026 PCE example, the screenshot says there was no consensus block and that July revisions were not reflected. I’d return explicit consensus\_status and revision\_status fields, plus source publication and observation timestamps, rather than simply omitting those values. For MCP selection, have you tested whether changing the FX Context tool description to mention “latest PCE” improves automatic invocation across a fixed prompt set?

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body:
That’s a very good point on explicit absence semantics. Right now the response effectively makes Claude infer state from missing fields, which is ambiguous. I like the distinction between `NOT_AVAILABLE` and `NOT_FOUND`, especially for consensus and revisions. I’m already storing publication/retrieval metadata, so surfacing that more explicitly in the MCP response would make the contract much clearer.

On tool selection, I’ve only done a small manual A/B so far:

* “What’s the latest US PCE?” → Claude answered without using the MCP
* “Use FX Context to get the latest US PCE.” → it invoked `get_event_context`

I haven’t yet run a fixed prompt set across different tool descriptions, but that’s probably the next useful test. I’m thinking of explicitly adding examples like “latest PCE”, “did CPI beat expectations?”, and “latest NFP” to the tool description and measuring whether invocation becomes more consistent.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
The A/B plan sounds right. A few things that tend to help with tool selection. Write the description around the user's phrasing, not the internal function, so include the questions people actually ask ("did CPI beat?", "what's the latest NFP?") as you're planning. Keep the names short and distinct, and say what it returns and when not to use it. Then run a fixed set of 30 to 50 prompts, including near-misses that shouldn't trigger it, and count invocation rate per description variant. Test across a couple of model versions too, since the behavior can shift.

On the data side, revisions are worth designing for early. PCE and most macro series get revised, so I'd keep every vintage with its own publication timestamp and let the response say which vintage it is. That keeps agents and backtests from using a revised number that wasn't available at the time. Similarly, keep the release time, the time you fetched it, and the source as separate fields, so a stale response is visible as stale.

For the consensus block, surfacing where it came from and when it was captured matters, since a consensus grabbed after the release is worthless for computing surprise.

We work on a similar problem at Cymetica with EventTrader, structured and timestamped events for agents, so I'm interested in how your absence semantics turn out.

Are you planning to log the model's outputs too, to check whether it ever contradicts the numbers you return?

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body:
Thanks — this is extremely useful.

The vintage point is especially important. I already treat consensus provenance carefully because a consensus captured after release would invalidate the surprise calculation, but I haven’t yet modeled revisions/vintages as explicitly as you describe. I agree that “latest value” alone is dangerous for both agents and backtests.

I’m leaning toward keeping publication time, retrieval time, source, and vintage identity separately, and eventually supporting an “as known at time T” view rather than silently returning revised history.

On tool selection, I like the idea of turning this into a proper regression suite rather than ad-hoc prompting. A fixed 30–50 prompt set with positive cases, near-misses and multiple model versions sounds like the right way to evaluate description changes.

For model outputs: the public MCP server currently logs tool calls/results, but it doesn’t see the host model’s final response. If I control the agent harness, I’d definitely like to log the tool result alongside the final model answer and check for contradictions or hallucinated numbers. I’d be hesitant to make that an assumption of the MCP itself, though.

EventTrader sounds very relevant to what I’m working on — I’ll take a look.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That all sounds right, and you're correct not to bake the contradiction check into the MCP, since it only sees tool calls and not the final answer. If you do run it in your own harness, a simple version is to extract every number from the model's reply and verify each one appears in the tool result (within rounding). That catches most invented figures cheaply. For the "as known at time T" view, test it with a case where a revision actually changed the headline number, so you know it returns the original and not the revised one. If you do look at EventTrader, I'd be interested to hear how it compares on the points above.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: Normalized, and for the reason you already found: the surprise math should never be the model's job. On the tool not being picked, it's usually the tool description. If it says what the service is rather than when to use it ("call this for any question about a US economic release, latest value, consensus or surprise"), Claude picks it much more reliably without you naming it.

replies.author: cocopierlab
replies.body:
That matches what I’m seeing. The MCP currently describes the capability reasonably well, but not strongly enough in terms of *when* the model should invoke it.

I’m going to rework the description around user intent — “latest value”, “actual vs consensus”, “beat/miss”, “surprise” — and add a few real prompt examples like “What’s the latest US PCE?”.

I also agree on keeping surprise calculation deterministic. I’d much rather have the MCP return a computed, provenance-backed surprise than ask the model to subtract and reason over possibly mismatched numbers.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that should do it. one more thing worth adding is a line on when not to call it, like general questions about what CPI is. that stops it firing on everything once the description gets broader.
